title: Overlapping subproblems

overview.what: A problem has overlapping subproblems if a naive recursive solution calls the same subproblem with the same arguments more than once.
overview.why: It tells you when caching (memoization) will speed up an algorithm, turning an exponential time complexity into polynomial time.

why_learning_this: It is the first diagnostic test to determine if Dynamic Programming will help.
You will learn to recognize why a simple recursive Fibonacci function is dangerously slow.

common_mistakes.title: Applying DP to all recursive problems
common_mistakes.explanation: Dynamic Programming only helps if subproblems overlap. Plain merge sort makes recursive calls, but each `(lo, hi)` pair is visited exactly once, so caching buys nothing.

recall_questions.q: What does it mean for a problem to have overlapping subproblems?
recall_questions.answer: A naive recursive solution calls the same subproblem with the same arguments multiple times.

practice_tasks.title: Add an operation counter
practice_tasks.prompt: Modify this naive Fibonacci function to increment a global counter every time it is called. See how fast the counter grows for `n=10` vs `n=20` to prove overlapping subproblems.

understanding_checks.question: Does Dynamic Programming speed up EVERY recursive algorithm? Why or why not?
understanding_checks.answer: No. Dynamic Programming only speeds up recursive algorithms that have overlapping subproblems. If each subproblem is distinct (like in merge sort), caching does nothing.
understanding_checks.why: Understanding when NOT to use DP is just as important as knowing how to use it.

understanding_checks.question: If you calculate `fib(5)` using naive recursion, how many times is `fib(2)` evaluated?
understanding_checks.why: `fib(5)` calls `fib(4)` and `fib(3)`. `fib(4)` calls `fib(3)` and `fib(2)`. The first `fib(3)` calls `fib(2)` and `fib(1)`. The second `fib(3)` calls `fib(2)` and `fib(1)`. Total: 3 times.

challenge.title: Identify Overlap
challenge.prompt: Look at the recursion tree for `fib(4)`. Write down the number of times `fib(1)` is called.
challenge.solution: `fib(4)` calls `fib(3)` and `fib(2)`. `fib(3)` calls `fib(2)` and `fib(1)`. `fib(2)` (from `fib(4)`) calls `fib(1)` and `fib(0)`. `fib(2)` (from `fib(3)`) calls `fib(1)` and `fib(0)`. `fib(1)` is called 3 times.
